chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said:

I heard Ibn Abi Layla saying: 'The blood money (diya) in the pre-Islamic period was one hundred camels, and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) confirmed this. Then he prescribed for the owners of cattle two hundred cows, and for the owners of sheep a thousand mature sheep, and for the owners of gold a thousand dinars, and for the owners of silver ten thousand dirhams, and for the cloth merchants of Yemen one hundred garments.'

Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj said: So I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about what Ibn Abi Layla had narrated, and he said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: The diya is one thousand dinars, and the value of a dinar is ten dirhams, and ten thousand dirhams for the people of the cities; and upon the Bedouin people the diya is one hundred camels; and for the people of the fertile lands two hundred cows or a thousand sheep.'

key_terms.الأمصار: Amsar — established cities/garrison towns; contrasted with bedouin (bawadi) and agricultural (sawad) communities
key_terms.الجاهلية: Jahiliyya — the pre-Islamic period of ignorance; used here to indicate that the 100-camel standard predated Islam
key_terms.الحلل: Hulal — fine garments or complete sets of clothing; a form of wealth in pre-Islamic Yemen
key_terms.الدية: Diya — the prescribed blood money paid in cases of killing or serious injury; an alternative to retaliation (qisas)
key_terms.السواد: Sawad — literally 'the black land'; refers to the fertile agricultural regions of Iraq/Mesopotamia

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on blood money (diya) and how does it vary by region and wealth?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal dispute between a Sunni jurist's (Ibn Abi Layla's) account of the Prophet's wergild (diya) rulings and Imam Sadiq's (AS) clarification citing Imam Ali's (AS) authoritative position. The hadith illustrates the early Islamic period's system of blood money, which varied according to the wealth and livelihood of the liable party — camels for Bedouins, cattle or sheep for agriculturalists, and gold/silver dinars for urban dwellers. Imam Ali's formulation establishes the dinar as the base unit (1000 dinars = 10,000 dirhams), providing a unified monetary standard that could be applied across diverse socioeconomic contexts.
